Part 2 · Inside a bank
Fig. 2.2 · interactive
Six words you'll hear in every AI meeting · click each
Model (LLM)
the engine
Prompt
the instruction
Context
what it can see
Hallucination
the risk
Grounding
the fix
Agent
the doer
Model
A large language model is a prediction engine trained on huge amounts of text. It writes the most likely next words, very well.
Everyday
The engine inside ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude.
In a bank
Banks pick
approved
models, often hosted privately, so client data never trains someone else's model.
Prompt
The instruction you give the model. A clear goal, context, format and examples get better answers.
Everyday
"Summarise this article in five bullet points for a busy manager."
In a bank
Citi's training teaches
"great prompting versus basic prompting"
. Experts finish in under 10 minutes, beginners in about 30.
Context
Everything the model can see when it answers: your prompt, attached files, the chat so far. It knows nothing else about your situation.
Everyday
Uploading your lecture notes so it answers about
your
course.
In a bank
Whatever you put in the context leaves your hands. That's why
data classification
rules exist.
Hallucination
When the model states something false, confidently. It isn't lying. It's predicting plausible words with no source behind them.
Everyday
A made-up citation in your essay that looks perfectly real.
In a bank
A wrong number in a client report is a
conduct issue
. The HKMA's own sandbox report calls hallucination a key concern.
Grounding
Making the model answer only from documents you trust, and show which line each answer came from. Often called RAG (retrieval-augmented generation).
Everyday
"Answer only from this PDF, and quote the page."
In a bank
The standard pattern:
approved content only, every answer cited
.
Agent
A model that can plan steps, use tools (search, files, email, code) and keep going until a goal is done.
Everyday
"Find three flights under HK$3,000 and put them in a table." It searches, compares and builds the table.
In a bank
The exciting part and the scary part.
Who approved what the agent did?

Part 2 · Check-in

A US bank uses generative AI to draft the credit memo for a loan. In April 2026 the regulators rewrote the model rulebook.
The answer · the rulebook shrank
The new rules
left generative AI out on purpose

Part 3 · Agents at work
Fig. 3.1 · interactive
Four building blocks · think of a new intern · click each
Block 1
Prompt
Telling the intern once
Block 2
Skill
The written procedure
Block 3
Plugin
The team's starter kit
Block 4
Agent
The intern who gets it done
What it is
An instruction you type into a chat. It works for that conversation, then it's gone. Next time you start again, and you'll phrase it differently.
Example
"Turn these meeting notes into a list of actions with owners and dates."
What it is
A saved file of instructions, and sometimes templates and scripts, that the AI loads when the task comes up.
Same steps, same checks, same format, every time.
You call it by name, like
/process-map
.
Example
A process-map skill: "Turn minutes into a flowchart. Cite the source line for every step. Never invent a date. Flag contradictions, don't fix them."
What it is
A package for a team: several skills plus
connections to the tools they need
(calendar, email, a database), and shortcut commands. Install once, the whole team works the same way.
Example
A "finance controllers" plugin with skills for reconciliations, variance commentary and month-end checklists, connected to the reporting system.
What it is
A model that
plans its own steps, uses tools and loops until the goal is met
. It picks which skills to use. It can work while you sleep.
Example
"Every night, read the family chat, pull out tasks and dates, and give me a briefing at 7am." That's my CHO, coming up in ten minutes.

Governance architecture.

DATA IN

Do not re-perform.
Validate.
In a world of infinite output, the scarce thing is
trust
. Design workflows that catch hallucinations.
Checkpoint 1 · human in the loop
A person approves before anything leaves.
Catches everything, but slow at scale
, so use it where a mistake would really hurt.
Checkpoint 2 · intent audit
Did it do what was asked?
Every claim has a source, totals reconcile, nothing outside scope.
This is where a second AI can check the first.
Checkpoint 3 · safety valve
Limits and an off switch
: a cap on value, who it may contact, and a way to stop it. My home agents in Part 3 run on rules like these.
My advice · skill 2 of 4
×
Tip 2 · from my MSBA talk
Tip 2: Build the currency of credibility.
True to your word once = trust. Persistently = credibility.
When anyone can generate a convincing answer, the person whose work is
checked, sourced and delivered as promised
is rare. Guard it, in a group project or a global bank.
This semester
Keep a "how I checked it" log.
Two lines for anything AI helped you make: what you checked, what you found.

Skill 4: The human moat
The unhackable skills.
High-stakes accountability
Somebody signs the recommendation and answers for it to a client or a regulator.
"The AI decided" is never accepted.
Trust & empathy
Clients buy from people they trust, especially when the news is bad.
A relationship is built over years, not generated.
Reading the room
Knowing what a client didn't say, when to stop talking, who in the meeting really decides.
None of it is in the data.
"Age of AI requires HUMAN connection."
84%
of new graduates say people skills matter more as AI spreads.
CFA Institute Graduate Outlook 2026
My advice · skill 4 of 4
×
Tip 4 · from my MSBA talk
Tip 4: Be the ultimate translator.
Connect first. Code second.
An LLM translates a prompt into code, or 100 pages into a summary. It can't sit with a team and hear the frustration they never say out loud.
That translation is yours.
This semester
Talk to one real user first.
Find a real frustration in a club, family business or internship before you build anything.
